chapter: Post office, day job and quitting
title: Sidney Cates job and bassist Jim Davis
summary: Sitting in with Sidney Cates' group; bassist Jim Davis's advice; other musicians in the post office.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: So, I mean, after that group broke up, I lost inches. I played a couple of times with a Tiffany Cates fan, he needed a piano player, asked me could I come help him out. I told him, Sidney, well you know I'm not playing anymore. He said, well come on, you can sing, maybe, just come on out and help me. He had a ball to play, and he said he needed a piano player. I don't know what happened to his regular piano player, so I went out and I played a couple times with him. But his group was all nice bunch of friendly stars and everything like that, but I mean, when you get used to playing, you like to get accustomed to the guys that you're around. Now, at one time, I had a bass player playing with me, Jim Davis. He used to play guitar.
He's playing with Fat Domino now.

A little short fella, he's playing bass with Fat Domino. Boy, he was a terrific bass player and a terrific help to me. He could stand right here, and after I played a few boards of a number, he said, next time you come around here, I want to tell you something. So, he said, now, instead of you making straight D, change the position and make it D minor. Let your F be right in the middle. I mean, all those kind of things he was telling you. Hear all those things. And he knew I could do it, because he told me, oh, he'd doubt me there'd be a whole lot better piano player if you just try, but you won't practice. I said, Jim, I just don't, you know, I mean, I didn't have any interest in it, because I had a decent job, and that night life, and trying to work all day, there's some of the cause in the post office that's doing it now, I don't remember. Kimball.
